sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E2375. Attribution follows local turn-taking, including interruptions within the identification anchors. U marks events containing inseparable speaker changes or genuinely ambiguous interjections. The transcript has transcription errors, censored words, and no reliable speaker labels; exact quotations preserve its wording. No edited teaser replay was identifiable.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: exactly the framework that religious people want to keep religion out of
candidates.explanation: Wolpe excludes an empirical framework when challenged about inherently insoluble mysteries. This could shelter an existence claim from relevant inquiry, but E683–691 recasts the mystery as enduring wonder compatible with understanding. The passage supplies an epistemic distinction, not a slogan; whether it excludes relevant contrary evidence remains unclear.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: I also think it's because civility is very religious virtue
candidates.explanation: After interruptions, Wolpe attributes his restraint to religion through a compact virtue claim. No reason establishes that religion explains this particular difference in conduct. Later arguments concern charity and goodness, not the asserted source of conversational civility. The joke rebukes behavior; it does not make disagreement itself proof of error.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: it's only not a moral action if you don't feel the unique expression of love
candidates.explanation: The response risks making rejection of blessing's moral status evidence that the critic lacks the relevant experience. However, E1087–1100 supplies personal testimony about familial love, and E1059–1072 concedes unbelievers' capacity to act. It is unclear whether experiential access shields a public moral claim or simply explains a practice's personal value.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: the remark gets melted by the heat of human anguish
candidates.explanation: The anguish metaphor suggests criticism loses standing at a grieving child's grave. Yet E1217–1237 offers an experiential reason for consolation's value, and E1240–1244 expressly acknowledges lack of empirical proof and continuing doubt. Whether suffering neutralizes truth-directed objections, rather than rebutting the dismissal of comfort as trivial, remains unclear.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: it is why it's always introduced as a time wasting TCH
candidates.explanation: Calling charity discussion always a time-wasting tactic dismisses its relevance without answering the current social-utility argument. Charity does not establish God's existence, as Wolpe concedes at E1665–1667; it does bear on E1622–1634. The blanket motive claim protects that exchange from contrary evidence, although Hitchens subsequently offers substantive counterexamples at E1678–1709.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: if God is dead then power is all that matters
candidates.explanation: The affirmation supplies the unearned move from purely evolved humanity to power and self-interest exhausting morality. E1916–1918 restates that conclusion. E2171–2198 later explains concern about human-made standards but does not establish that secular reasons reduce to power. E1921–1926 fairly clarifies that Wolpe accepts evolution and disputes its exhaustiveness.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: I don't believe people have doubts about it would tell them to someone
candidates.explanation: Hitchens discounts reported belief by proposing concealed doubt, potentially sheltering his interpretation from contrary survey responses. But E2303–2315 grounds it in his experience, and E2340–2346 accepts a different survey. This is a limited hypothesis about reporting behavior; the text does not establish unrestricted rejection of every unfavorable result.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: if Christopher says to me God doesn't exist and I say but we do good things he's got a point
contrasts.explanation: Wolpe explicitly separates evidence of social usefulness from evidence of God's existence, then identifies which preceding claim his charity argument addressed. This is a relevant, qualified distinction rather than an affirmation replacing reasons.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: it still doesn't mean that there's a God who takes sides answers prayers
contrasts.explanation: Hitchens distinguishes a first cause from an intervening deity and expressly concedes that he cannot refute the former assumption. The concise conclusion identifies an additional inference requiring support rather than claiming to have disproved every conception of God.
